articles.title: Reclaiming Indigenous culinary histories in Nepal
articles.summary: Sanjib Chaudhary of Global Voices caught up with Binti Gurung,  a food historian and founder of Natural Roots Foundation, to talk about her work on the food heritage of Nepal.
articles.content:
Food enriches our soul. It makes us who we are. However, the emergence of cosmopolitanism and global and local food politics has sidelined Indigenous food, not to mention the traditions and rituals associated with them.

“Over the last decades, ever since the country was opened up to the outside world in the 1950s, in search of a national food identity, the staple daal bhaat, a nutrient-dense combination of lentils and rice accompanied by vegetables, has been elevated to Nepal’s national dish,” writes Binti Gurung, a food historian and founder of Natural Roots Foundation, an organization dedicated to documenting, preserving, and promoting Indigenous Himalayan food heritage, traditional recipes, and local knowledge in Nepal. “The national food narrative that is being set completely obscures the varied regional histories and food practices of the Indigenous peoples.”

The Foundation, established in 2017, promotes the many varieties of food that have become neglected in Nepal, especially the plants and herbs that can be foraged in the forests and mountains.

Working with Aama Samuha, a collective of women’s groups set up to maintain cultural traditions and support communal activities in Nepali villages, she has been documenting and archiving the food knowledge primarily held by Indigenous women in Nepal.

The Lekhali Cookbook, authored by Gurung, draws its name from lekh, the high ridges in Nepal, and highlights the rich food tradition shared by women’s groups from Nepal’s Mustang, Manang, Lamjung, and Gorkha districts.

Sanjib Chaudhary of Global Voices caught up with Binti Gurung to talk about her work on food heritage. The interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Sanjib Chaudhary (SC): Can you introduce yourself and tell us a bit about your work?

Binti Gurung (BG): Before talking about the food heritage of Nepal, it’s necessary to mention that knowing the broader political and historical context of the country is important because a lot of what my work looks into connects with understanding of the past.

The pivotal moment can be attributed to the 1950s, when the absolutist regime came to an end. As a country, Nepal had remained closed off to the outside world for so long that very little was understood about Nepali society, particularly its food practices.

Within this environment of reaching out to the past events that happened in this land, uncovering the stories of the people, and mainly breaking down and deconstructing the idea of “Nepali-ness,” lies the understanding of our food heritage.

I myself come from what used to be called a Gurung country until the 1970s. I know something about our collective history as Gurung people, and that my great-grandfather on the maternal side was a mukhiya, a tribal chief somewhere in that Gurung country. There are no written documents about our lineage, apart from the knowledge that remains in the tongue. I take pride in that, but it also means some knowledge has not been transmitted.

My paternal grandfather was the first person to be educated because of his connection to British India, after which he did a lot in his village, which included donating some of his personal land to the village school. Whereas I am the first in my family to go to university, learn English (like the rest of my generation), and read history.

SC: Food sovereignty is a burning issue for Indigenous peoples. Can you give us an overview of what challenges Indigenous communities in Nepal are facing with regard to food sovereignty?

BG: Even though the constitution of 2015 has given recognition to the right to food, how does it translate to the many Indigenous groups accessing their food? Are the Indigenous peoples who have been living by the rivers and the forests able to access the foods that they have learned to process, collect, and eat?

For the communities that still live in or near the forest, how are their relationships affected when forests are turned into national parks? Do the Indigenous peoples who have been relying on these ancestral food practices have access? Can the state recognize and permit it?

When we start to think this way, we go beyond the conversation about food sovereignty because then we have to talk about the land and the peoples who inhabit it, and their connection to it.

SC: Nepal is a multi-ethnic country, and communities have their own food and agriculture systems. However, food politics is prevalent, with some communities claiming a particular dish as solely theirs. What’s your take on this?

BG: I think it is impossible to claim any particular dish as solely belonging to only one community. After all, we live in a shared world. We are beings in constant interaction with the land. Like any living practice that is evolving, our food practices are also in motion; it is not a static, fixed thing.

What may be helpful is to think about how a dish or food practice evolved. Or even to try to understand how it has evolved the way it has, including the factors of influence. Even though we think of Nepali communities having their own food systems, if we look underneath somewhere, we can find some similar practices.

One example is the way food is harvested from the forest; this particular practice, whether in the high mountains, hills, or the Terai, remains similar. Of course, how this practice is treated by those not practicing is an entirely different thing.

SC: It’s high time we promote Indigenous food in a global space. Can you tell us about your recent book “The Lekhali Cookbook: Indigenous Food Heritage from the Highlands of Nepal” and the dishes you’d like to share with a wider audience?

BG: This book has been in the making for a very long time. When I started doing this work in 2017, at some point it felt very urgent to understand the issues around it, and gradually it became important to start documenting in a written way because a lot had been unknown.

There may be many factors why the conversation around food heritage has remained so obscure, but one that I attribute strongly to is our own political history that has shaped the Indigenous experiences.

For many Indigenous communities, the problem has also been due to others writing about their history. Of course, there are some very rare scholars who have done a fine job, but in the case of our own history, there is now an immense effort to establish or re-establish our origin account. It’s very saddening to have to read about some of these accounts. And then there is also the process of verifying and fact-checking, and that takes a lot of time.

The Lekhali Cookbook came into being due to a generous grant from the British Council. A lot of the work had been conducted prior to receiving the grant, but it allowed us to visit the villages in the central Himalayas and work with aama samuha [translated as “mothers’ groups,” acting as local women’s collectives] who are heavily involved in the food production process. Based on the consultation with the groups, we collected the recipes of the eight villages of Lamjung, Manang, Mustang, and Gorkha.

In the book, we have some unique recipes that many people do not know, such as the foraged panyu (wild rhubarb), kru (yak sausage), yak curry with satu, or farsi ko bhat eaten with sattu up in the high Gorkha hills.

SC: What do you think the future of Indigenous food will look like in a decade's time? What should Indigenous communities, in your opinion, do to preserve and promote their food heritage?

BG: I think we have immense challenges ahead of us. Every year, these challenges seem to be only growing more and more. We only have to look at the recent disasters; it’s quite terrifying for the people who are living in these landscapes.

For several reasons, it’s crucial that we recognize that our situation is changing and that it is very fragile, and we have to be alert to this changing situation. So much has already changed, and within this framework we have to think of how we are going to adapt to our new circumstances, whether it is living in the city, establishing a relationship with urban life, learning to operate in a language that is not your mother tongue, learning technology, issues of sustainability, and so on.

In the midst of this vast change from our previous ancestral way of life, how are we going to hold ourselves as people with a distinct way of living, language, and culture? Moreover, how are we going to maintain the values that have been passed down to us from our ancestors? How willing are we to work for our collective welfare to protect our cultural and food heritage in this sea of change? Because without addressing these questions or without internalizing them, we cannot have real progress.

articles.personality_title: Preserving Nepal’s Indigenous food traditions through community and culture

**Context** – Nepal is a country with many different ethnic groups, each with its own food traditions. Since the 1950s, the focus has been on one national dish, daal bhaat, which has overshadowed many Indigenous foods and practices. This has made it harder for Indigenous communities to keep their unique food heritage alive.

**What happened** – Binti Gurung, a food historian and founder of the Natural Roots Foundation, is working to document and protect the traditional foods of Nepal’s Indigenous peoples. Since 2017, her foundation has collected recipes and knowledge, especially from women’s groups called Aama Samuha in mountain villages. Gurung also published "The Lekhali Cookbook," featuring rare recipes from Nepal’s highland regions, to share these foods with more people.

**Impact** – This work helps preserve important cultural knowledge that is at risk of being lost. It supports Indigenous women who hold much of this food wisdom and raises awareness about the connection between food, land, and identity. The cookbook introduces unique dishes like wild rhubarb and yak sausage, which many outside these communities have never seen. It also highlights challenges Indigenous people face in accessing traditional foods due to changes like forest protections.

This work may inspire more efforts to protect and celebrate Indigenous food cultures in Nepal and beyond.

articles.title: The ongoing efforts to get ecocide recognized at the International Criminal Court
articles.summary: For the nations that started this, the stakes are not abstract. They are asking the world to build infrastructure to prosecute and prevent harm that is already happening to them.
articles.content:
This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In September 2024, Vanuatu, Fiji, and Samoa filed an amendment request at the International Criminal Court (ICC) to get “ecocide” recognized as a crime under international law. The ICC currently recognizes four criminal categories: genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and the crime of aggression.

Over two years later, the amendment is still formally pending; but that does not mean environmental activists are waiting around — in fact, many are working both in the public eye and behind the scenes to establish legal infrastructure to protect the environment, combat the climate crisis, and punish those responsible for defiling the planet.

Read more: Pacific island nations want ecocide to be an international crime

According to an independent expert panel convened by the Stop Ecocide Foundation, ecocide is legally defined as “unlawful or wanton acts committed with knowledge that there is a substantial likelihood of severe and either widespread or long-term damage to the environment being caused by those acts.”

For the countries that backed the proposal, the climate crisis is not an abstract threat; it is a real and present danger with active consequences for their people.

In 2021, Simon Kofe, Tuvalu’s Minister for Justice, Communication and Foreign Affairs, gave a presentation at the international COP26 conference on climate change while standing in knee-deep water to demonstrate how rising sea levels threaten low-lying island nations. Tuvaluan officials are also exploring ways to become the first “digital nation” as a backup plan in case rising sea levels submerge all livable land in the archipelago. In Fiji alone, six villages have already been relocated because of climate change, with others in progress and dozens more under assessment. As Vanuatu’s Special Envoy for Climate Change and Environment, Ralph Regenvanu, says, climate damage is “devastating our island economy, submerging our territory, and threatening livelihoods.”

Shortly after the amendment was submitted, it was also backed by the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), which is experiencing increasingly deadly flooding as well as air quality issues related to exploitative mining operations.

It is not a coincidence that those who are pushing hardest for these legal mechanisms are those most affected by the climate crisis. These nations did little to cause the crisis, while major superpowers like the U.S., China, and Europe, as well as the corporations that bolster them, have made billions by exploiting and polluting the environment unchecked.

Meanwhile, those who suffer from the consequences of our eroding climate have limited legal recourse against the corporations and states most responsible. This juxtaposition is where the argument to make ecocide an international crime comes in.

Vanuatu was the first state to call for ecocide to be added to the ICC in 2019. In announcing the proposal, Regenvanu said:

“We are taking bold and necessary action to address these challenges and encourage other vulnerable states to take note of our newly tabled proposal to bring ecocide to the ICC. Legal recognition of severe and widespread environmental harm holds significant potential to ensure justice and, crucially, to deter further destruction.”

Why reform the ICC?

The International Criminal Court was formally established in 2002 to prosecute individuals for grave international crimes (not to be confused with the International Court of Justice, which settles legal disputes between countries).

Environmental crimes are particularly tricky, as traditional legal accountability measures tend to rely on specific individuals or property that have been harmed in order to pursue legal action. In cases where polluters are contributing to a broader destructive pattern, the legal standing becomes murky. This theory has been tested numerous times as individuals have sought to sue fossil fuel companies in civil court for their destructive practices and malfeasance, with most cases largely unsuccessful.

Supporters say that if the proposed amendment were successful, it would give ICC prosecutors the power to hold individuals, such as the executives of large polluting companies or heads of state, responsible in cases like massive oil spills or the deforestation of essential rainforests.

As an editorial in The Global Witness notes:

While there have been a series of recent valiant attempts to sue fossil fuel corporations in civil court for covering up evidence that their activities were causing global warming, the defendants have largely been able to get away scot-free. … Criminalizing ecocide would fill this legal gap, and allow individuals (and companies in some jurisdictions) to be prosecuted for engaging in acts with knowledge that they are substantially likely to damage the environment, without the need to show harm to any individual person.

To add a crime to the Rome Statute, a proposal must win a two-thirds majority vote within the court’s Assembly of States Parties. Even then, an amendment to the statute’s crimes provisions would bind only the states that accept it, and the court could not prosecute nationals or territory of states that do not.

The Rome Statute has 123 signatory parties — a number that does not include China, India, or the U.S., the world’s three largest contributors to greenhouse gas emissions. The U.S., in particular, under current President Donald Trump’s administration, has backed away from climate commitments in recent years, including withdrawing from the UN’s 2015 Paris Climate Agreement. It has also become increasingly hostile toward the court itself, as the Trump administration imposed sanctions on individual ICC prosecutors and judges beginning in early 2025. Then, in a September 2026 address to the UN General Assembly, Trump urged all member states to withdraw from the treaty altogether, and, weeks later, in October 2026, he imposed sweeping sanctions on the court itself.

With the biggest emitters outside the court, and Washington working to undermine it, advocates are looking beyond The Hague and ICC reform. As legal watchdogs argue, the end goal is not merely to get the ICC to recognize ecocide — though that would be an excellent first step — rather, if the ICC were to establish a framework for prosecuting international environmental crimes, through an amendment or merely by adapting its existing policies, this could push ratifying states to update their domestic penal codes and adopt policies to protect and preserve their own ecosystems, and also prosecute those who violate them.

Existing provisions within the Rome Statute

Even though the proposal has thus far not been adopted by the ICC, the court has not stood still.

In December 2025, ICC prosecutors published a policy paper on prosecuting environmental damage through the pre-existing mechanisms already laid out in the Rome Statute — the international treaty which established the ICC.

The Rome Statute mentions the environment exactly one time. Article 8(2)(b)(iv) makes it a war crime to launch an attack knowing it will cause “widespread, long-term and severe” damage to the environment. Traditionally, this article has applied only during armed conflict, and previous attempts to prosecute environmental destruction at the court have been unsuccessful.

Vanuatu’s ambassador to the UN, Odo Tevi, has argued that the reckless destruction of nature “can and does take place at any time, not just during conflict.”

The December 2025 policy, launched at the Assembly of States Parties, was co-hosted by Costa Rica, France, Germany, Panama, and the Marshall Islands. It explains how environmental destruction can be investigated and prosecuted within the four existing crime categories, for example, when pollution or the seizure of natural resources is used to commit a crime against humanity.

Analysts at the Conflict and Environment Observatory note that this policy paper does not address the ecocide proposal and that ambiguity in the war crime standard remains. Others point to limited resources at the prosecutor’s office.

In September 2026, ICC representatives said they had “moved into the implementation stage” to establish clearer parameters for prosecuting environmental crimes under the Rome Statute. In its statement, the office said it had received numerous communications about alleged crimes with an environmental dimension and was building a network of environmental law enforcement authorities, relevant organizations, expert groups, and civil society organizations to investigate.

But some jurisdictions are not waiting. As one recent study notes, “the substance of ecocide criminalization has advanced everywhere except through the amendment: an EU directive whose gravest offense is officially ‘comparable to “ecocide,”’ a Council of Europe convention, national codes in Belgium, France and Ukraine, and a completed OTP [ICC’s Office of the Prosecutor] policy that prosecutes environmental damage through the existing four crimes.”

Counts vary depending on how many states currently employ domestic laws against ecocide. Stop Ecocide International says twelve countries, including Belgium, France, and Ukraine, have adopted ecocide or equivalent offenses into domestic law. Mauritius became the most recent in April 2026, and legislation is progressing in countries including Brazil, Peru, Argentina, Mexico, Italy, and the Netherlands. As noted in the aforementioned study, the EU’s revised Environmental Crime Directive also covers conduct “comparable to ecocide,” and member states had to transpose it by May 2026.

What comes next

The next stage is procedural rather than dramatic: Whether states give the proposal a formal path forward at the Assembly of States Parties’ 25th session in The Hague, from November 30 to December 7, 2026. A vote would signal whether the Rome Statute can grow beyond the atrocities it was written for. A stall would leave the prosecutor’s policy and national laws as the main tools available.

The decision comes at a crucial time for the ICC, as some international stakeholders begin to question the legitimacy, power, and effectiveness of international ruling bodies.

For the nations that started this, the stakes are not abstract. They are asking the world to build infrastructure to prosecute and prevent harm that is already happening to them. Until that infrastructure is implemented, the burden of harm will continue to fall on those least responsible for causing this crisis.

The story is focused, detailed, and highlights meaningful progress and advocacy with potential large-scale positive impact.
articles.personality_title: Pacific nations push to make ecocide an international crime at the ICC
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Some small island countries and others affected by climate change want the International Criminal Court (ICC) to recognize “ecocide” as a crime. Ecocide means serious harm to the environment caused by people who know their actions will damage nature badly and for a long time. Right now, the ICC can only punish genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity, and aggression.

**What happened** – In September 2024, Vanuatu, Fiji, and Samoa asked the ICC to add ecocide to its list of crimes. The Democratic Republic of Congo also supports this. These countries face real dangers from climate change, like rising seas and flooding. For example, Tuvalu’s minister showed how rising water threatens his country by standing in knee-deep water at a climate meeting. Fiji has already moved six villages because of climate damage. The ICC has not yet decided on the proposal, but is working on ways to use its current rules to punish environmental harm.

**Impact** – If ecocide becomes a crime, leaders and company bosses who cause big environmental damage could be held responsible by an international court. This is important because many polluters have escaped punishment so far. It would help protect nature and the people who suffer most from climate change, especially when local laws are not strong enough. Some countries, like Belgium and France, are already making ecocide illegal at home.

**What's next step** – In late 2026, the ICC’s member countries will vote on whether to officially consider adding ecocide as a crime. Even if the vote is delayed or rejected, the ICC plans to keep using its current rules to fight environmental crimes. Meanwhile, more countries may pass their own laws against ecocide. The vote will show if the ICC is ready to expand its role to protect the planet.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Small island nations and others are leading a global effort to make serious environmental harm an international crime, aiming to hold polluters accountable and better protect vulnerable communities from climate damage.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les nations du Pacifique veulent faire de l’écocide un crime international à la CPI
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Certains petits pays insulaires et d’autres touchés par le changement climatique souhaitent que la Cour pénale internationale (CPI) reconnaisse « l’écocide » comme un crime. L’écocide désigne les graves dommages causés à l’environnement par des actes commis en sachant qu’ils provoqueront une destruction importante et durable de la nature. Actuellement, la CPI peut seulement punir le génocide, les crimes de guerre, les crimes contre l’humanité et l’agression.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – En septembre 2024, Vanuatu, Fidji et Samoa ont demandé à la CPI d’ajouter l’écocide à la liste des crimes. La République démocratique du Congo soutient aussi cette demande. Ces pays font face à de réels dangers liés au changement climatique, comme la montée des eaux et les inondations. Par exemple, le ministre des affaires étrangères de Tuvalu a montré la menace de la montée des eaux en se tenant dans l’eau jusqu’aux genoux lors d’une conférence internationale. Fidji a déjà déplacé six villages à cause des dégâts climatiques. La CPI n’a pas encore pris de décision sur la proposition, mais travaille à utiliser ses règles actuelles pour punir les atteintes à l’environnement.

**Impact** – Si l’écocide devient un crime, les dirigeants et patrons d’entreprises qui causent de graves dommages à l’environnement pourraient être tenus responsables devant une cour internationale. Cela est important car beaucoup de pollueurs ont échappé jusqu’ici à toute sanction. Cela aiderait à protéger la nature et les populations les plus touchées par le changement climatique, surtout quand les lois locales sont insuffisantes. Certains pays, comme la Belgique et la France, ont déjà rendu l’écocide illégal sur leur territoire.

**Prochaine étape** – Fin 2026, les pays membres de la CPI voteront pour décider si l’écocide peut officiellement devenir un crime. Même si le vote est retardé ou rejeté, la CPI prévoit de continuer à utiliser ses règles actuelles pour lutter contre les crimes environnementaux. En attendant, d’autres pays pourraient adopter leurs propres lois contre l’écocide. Ce vote montrera si la CPI est prête à étendre son rôle pour protéger la planète.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Des nations insulaires et d’autres pays mènent un effort mondial pour faire de la destruction grave de l’environnement un crime international, afin de tenir les pollueurs responsables et mieux protéger les communautés vulnérables aux dégâts climatiques.
articles.personality_title_es: Naciones del Pacífico impulsan que el ecocidio sea un crimen internacional en la CPI
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Algunos países insulares pequeños y otros afectados por el cambio climático quieren que la Corte Penal Internacional (CPI) reconozca el “ecocidio” como un crimen. El ecocidio significa un daño grave al medio ambiente causado por personas que saben que sus acciones dañarán la naturaleza de forma severa y duradera. Ahora, la CPI solo puede castigar genocidio, crímenes de guerra, crímenes contra la humanidad y agresión.

**Qué pasó** – En septiembre de 2024, Vanuatu, Fiji y Samoa pidieron a la CPI que agregue el ecocidio a su lista de crímenes. También lo apoya la República Democrática del Congo. Estos países enfrentan peligros reales por el cambio climático, como el aumento del nivel del mar y las inundaciones. Por ejemplo, el ministro de Tuvalu mostró la amenaza del agua creciente al pararse con agua hasta las rodillas en una reunión climática. Fiji ya ha trasladado seis aldeas por daños climáticos. La CPI aún no decide sobre la propuesta, pero trabaja para usar sus reglas actuales para castigar daños ambientales.

**Impacto** – Si el ecocidio se convierte en un crimen, líderes y jefes de empresas que causen daños graves al ambiente podrían ser responsabilizados en una corte internacional. Esto es importante porque muchos contaminadores han evitado castigo hasta ahora. Ayudaría a proteger la naturaleza y a las personas que sufren más por el cambio climático, especialmente cuando las leyes locales no son fuertes. Algunos países, como Bélgica y Francia, ya han hecho ilegal el ecocidio en sus territorios.

**Próximo paso** – A finales de 2026, los países miembros de la CPI votarán para decidir si el ecocidio se convierte oficialmente en un crimen. Aunque la votación se retrase o rechace, la CPI planea seguir usando sus reglas actuales para combatir crímenes ambientales. Mientras tanto, más países pueden aprobar sus propias leyes contra el ecocidio. La votación mostrará si la CPI está lista para ampliar su papel en la protección del planeta.

**Resumen en una frase** – Naciones insulares y otros países lideran un esfuerzo global para convertir el daño grave al medio ambiente en un crimen internacional, buscando responsabilizar a los contaminadores y proteger mejor a las comunidades vulnerables al cambio climático.

articles.title: ‘You will not be alone’: General Assembly President tells Rohingya refugees after genocide ruling
articles.summary: A day after the UN’s highest court found that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya, the President of the General Assembly visited the refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, urging the world to turn the landmark judgement into action.
articles.content: A day after the UN’s highest court found that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya, the President of the General Assembly visited the refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, urging the world to turn the landmark judgement into action.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories
articles.reasoning: The UN's highest court ruling recognizing genocide against the Rohingya is a significant human rights milestone with broad implications for justice and accountability. The General Assembly President's visit to refugee camps and call for action highlights a meaningful step toward addressing and remedying a grave humanitarian crisis affecting a large population.
articles.personality_title: UN General Assembly President visits Rohingya refugees after genocide ruling
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The United Nations’ highest court recently ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, a Muslim minority group. This ruling came after years of violence and persecution that forced many Rohingya to flee their homes.

**What happened** – One day after the court’s decision, the President of the UN General Assembly traveled to refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. There, he met with Rohingya refugees and encouraged the international community to take real action based on the court’s judgement.

**Impact** – This visit shows the world’s attention is focused on helping the Rohingya people. The court’s ruling is important because it officially recognizes the crimes against the Rohingya, opening the door for justice and support. The President’s call for action stresses the need to improve conditions in the camps and work toward lasting solutions.

**What’s next step** – Following this visit, countries and organizations are expected to increase aid and support for the Rohingya refugees. The ruling may also lead to legal actions against those responsible for the genocide. Continued international pressure could help protect the Rohingya and prevent similar tragedies.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The UN’s genocide ruling and the General Assembly President’s visit mark important steps toward justice and support for Rohingya refugees.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le président de l’Assemblée générale de l’ONU visite les réfugiés rohingyas après le jugement sur le génocide
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La plus haute juridiction des Nations Unies a récemment jugé que le Myanmar avait commis un génocide contre les Rohingyas, un groupe minoritaire musulman. Ce jugement fait suite à des années de violences et de persécutions qui ont forcé de nombreux Rohingyas à fuir leur pays.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Un jour après cette décision, le président de l’Assemblée générale de l’ONU s’est rendu dans les camps de réfugiés de Cox’s Bazar, au Bangladesh. Il a rencontré les réfugiés rohingyas et a exhorté la communauté internationale à agir concrètement suite à ce jugement.

**Impact** – Cette visite montre que le monde porte attention aux Rohingyas. Le jugement est important car il reconnaît officiellement les crimes commis contre eux, ouvrant la voie à la justice et au soutien. L’appel à l’action du président souligne la nécessité d’améliorer les conditions dans les camps et de chercher des solutions durables.

**Prochaine étape** – Après cette visite, on attend une augmentation de l’aide et du soutien des pays et des organisations aux réfugiés rohingyas. Le jugement pourrait aussi entraîner des poursuites contre les responsables du génocide. La pression internationale continue pourrait aider à protéger les Rohingyas et à éviter de nouvelles tragédies.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Le jugement sur le génocide et la visite du président de l’Assemblée générale marquent des étapes importantes vers la justice et le soutien aux réfugiés rohingyas.
articles.personality_title_es: Presidente de la Asamblea General de la ONU visita a refugiados rohingyas tras fallo de genocidio
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El tribunal más alto de las Naciones Unidas determinó recientemente que Myanmar cometió genocidio contra los rohingyas, un grupo minoritario musulmán. Esta decisión llega después de años de violencia y persecución que obligaron a muchos rohingyas a huir de sus hogares.

**Qué pasó** – Un día después del fallo, el Presidente de la Asamblea General de la ONU visitó los campos de refugiados en Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. Allí se reunió con los refugiados rohingyas y pidió a la comunidad internacional que actúe basándose en esta decisión.

**Impacto** – Esta visita muestra que el mundo está prestando atención a la situación de los rohingyas. El fallo es importante porque reconoce oficialmente los crímenes cometidos, lo que abre la puerta a la justicia y al apoyo. El llamado del Presidente a la acción destaca la necesidad de mejorar las condiciones en los campos y buscar soluciones duraderas.

**Próximo paso** – Tras esta visita, se espera que los países y organizaciones aumenten la ayuda y el apoyo a los refugiados rohingyas. El fallo también podría llevar a acciones legales contra los responsables del genocidio. La presión internacional continua podría ayudar a proteger a los rohingyas y prevenir tragedias similares.

**Frase clave** – El fallo de genocidio y la visita del Presidente de la Asamblea General representan pasos importantes hacia la justicia y el apoyo a los refugiados rohingyas.

articles.title: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?
articles.summary: The agreement will allow young people between 18 and 31 year-olds to travel, work or study in the EU for up to three years.
articles.content:
The UK and EU have agreed a youth experience scheme which will allow a limited number of 18 to 31-year-olds to work, study or travel in the European Union for up to three years.

Every year, 100,000 Britons will be able to participate in the scheme, with a reciprocal arrangement for 100,000 EU citizens.

A joint EU-UK statement says the scheme is due to launch no later than January 2030.

The numbers for both those coming to and from the EU will be allocated among the member nations according to each country's population.

UK participants will initially be able to apply to travel to one particular EU country but can later switch to a different one, staying in a total of three countries during their three-year stay. However, they must spend 12 months in one country before switching.

Visas issued by the EU or the UK will initially be valid for two years, with an option to extend for one more year.

Neither UK nor EU citizens will be able to access benefits while abroad or bring dependants such as children.

Participants will need to pay an application fee and prove they have enough money to support themselves during their stay.

There are currently no details on what application fees UK citizens will have to pay, but the EU currently charges €90 (£75) for short-term visas. Numbers vary between countries for longer-term stays.

The UK charges £340 for its other youth mobility schemes, in addition to a £776 annual health surcharge.

The UK government has not said how much money an EU or UK national needs to have access to in order to take part but for similar schemes the figure is £2,530.

There are no details yet on how places on the scheme will be allocated if it is oversubscribed; however previous schemes have used either a first-come, first-served basis or a random ballot system.

The UK already has youth mobility schemes in place with other countries, including 45,000 places for Australians, 8,500 for New Zealanders and 1,000 for Icelanders.

In 2024, 24,400 out of a possible total of 81,100 youth mobility scheme visas were issued by the UK.

Speaking at a joint press conference with EU leaders, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "These opportunities open horizons, and they create friendships that will last a lifetime.

"So it's a very emotional moment because these are the young people that will shape our future."
articles.reasoning: The article describes a new EU-UK youth experience scheme that will allow a significant number of young people to travel, work, and study across borders, fostering cultural exchange and personal development. This agreement has broad societal benefits by enhancing opportunities for youth mobility and international cooperation, with clear details on the scheme's scope and implementation.
articles.personality_title: New EU-UK youth scheme to let 100,000 young people work and study abroad each year
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The UK and the European Union have agreed on a new program to help young people travel, work, or study in each other's countries. This comes after years of changing travel rules following Brexit.

**What happened** – Starting by January 2030, 100,000 young people aged 18 to 31 from the UK can live, work, or study in the EU for up to three years. At the same time, 100,000 young people from EU countries can do the same in the UK. Participants will first apply to one country but can move to two others during their stay, spending at least one year in each.

**Impact** – This scheme is important because it gives young people more chances to explore new cultures, gain work experience, and study abroad without complicated visa problems. It also strengthens connections between the UK and EU through people-to-people exchanges, helping young people build friendships and skills across borders.

**What's next step** – The program will open applications before January 2030. Details like visa fees and how to apply will become clearer over time. Officials will also decide how to choose participants if more people want to join than spots available.

**One-sentence takeaway** – From 2030, 100,000 young people yearly can live, work, or study across the UK and EU, opening new doors for travel and learning.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un nouveau programme jeunesse UE-Royaume-Uni pour travailler et étudier à l’étranger
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le Royaume-Uni et l’Union européenne ont conclu un accord pour permettre aux jeunes de voyager, travailler ou étudier dans leurs pays respectifs, après des années de règles de voyage compliquées liées au Brexit.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Dès janvier 2030, 100 000 jeunes âgés de 18 à 31 ans du Royaume-Uni pourront vivre, travailler ou étudier dans l’UE jusqu’à trois ans. En même temps, 100 000 jeunes de l’UE pourront faire de même au Royaume-Uni. Les participants postuleront d’abord pour un pays, mais pourront ensuite en changer deux fois, en restant au moins un an dans chaque pays.

**Impact** – Ce programme est important car il offre aux jeunes plus d’opportunités pour découvrir de nouvelles cultures, acquérir de l’expérience professionnelle et étudier à l’étranger sans problèmes de visa compliqués. Il renforce aussi les liens entre le Royaume-Uni et l’UE grâce aux échanges entre les jeunes.

**Prochaine étape** – Les candidatures ouvriront avant janvier 2030. Les détails sur les frais de visa et les procédures seront précisés. Les autorités décideront aussi comment choisir les participants si la demande dépasse les places disponibles.

**Résumé en une phrase** – À partir de 2030, 100 000 jeunes par an pourront vivre, travailler ou étudier entre le Royaume-Uni et l’UE, ouvrant de nouvelles opportunités de voyage et d’apprentissage.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo programa juvenil UE-Reino Unido para trabajar y estudiar en el extranjero
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El Reino Unido y la Unión Europea han acordado un programa para que los jóvenes puedan viajar, trabajar o estudiar en los países del otro, tras años de reglas complicadas por el Brexit.

**Qué pasó** – Desde enero de 2030, 100,000 jóvenes de 18 a 31 años del Reino Unido podrán vivir, trabajar o estudiar en la UE hasta por tres años. Al mismo tiempo, 100,000 jóvenes de la UE podrán hacer lo mismo en el Reino Unido. Los participantes aplicarán primero a un país, pero luego podrán cambiar a dos más, pasando al menos un año en cada uno.

**Impacto** – Este programa es importante porque da a los jóvenes más oportunidades para conocer nuevas culturas, ganar experiencia laboral y estudiar en el extranjero sin problemas complicados de visa. También fortalece las conexiones entre el Reino Unido y la UE mediante intercambios entre personas.

**Próximo paso** – Las solicitudes se abrirán antes de enero de 2030. Se aclararán detalles sobre tarifas de visa y cómo aplicar. También decidirán cómo elegir a los participantes si hay más solicitudes que lugares disponibles.

**Resumen en una frase** – Desde 2030, 100,000 jóvenes cada año podrán vivir, trabajar o estudiar entre el Reino Unido y la UE, abriendo nuevas oportunidades de viaje y aprendizaje.
